findings.title: Minimum token schema strips all fields except access_token
findings.body: The computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` do not create wildcard/ passthrough keys; they create the same literal property name. Zod objects strip unknown keys by default, so in sharing mode `refresh_token`, `expires_in`, `expiry_date`, `scope`, `token_type` and provider-specific fields are removed from `data`. Callers then compute expiry from a missing `expires_in` (e.g. Zoom `Date.now() + undefined*1000` = NaN) and lose the real refresh token, corrupting the refreshed credential.

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with literal string "refresh_token"
findings.body: When the parsed response has no `refresh_token` (always the case in sharing mode because the schema strips it, and possible in normal mode where it is optional), this line sets `data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Callers such as Zoom and Webex copy that value into the stored credential key, so the database now contains a bogus refresh token and any later non-synced refresh will fail with invalid_grant.

findings.title: Synced branch returns raw fetch Response incompatible with most callers
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens` returns `refreshFunction()` in the normal branch but a raw `fetch` Response in the synced branch. Callers expect incompatible shapes: Google expects `res.data`, HubSpot expects a `HubspotToken` object with `accessToken`/`expiresIn`, and Zoho Bigin/ZohoCRM/HubSpot expect Axios-style `.data`. In synced mode those properties are undefined, causing crashes (`token.access_token` on undefined) or storing a serialized Response/NaN expiry and destroying the credential. Only fetch-based callers can work with this return value.

findings.title: SafeParse result object is stored as the credential key
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the Zod SafeParse result `{success, data}`, but this line assigns it directly as `key` and persists it with `prisma.credential.update`. Previously `googleCredentialSchema.parse()` returned the credential itself. The next load does `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` on `{success:true,data:{...}}`, which fails, and the stored access/refresh tokens are nested under `data` instead of at the top level, breaking Google Calendar after the first refresh.

findings.title: Google refresh assumes synced response has `.data`
findings.body: In synced mode `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a fetch `Response`, which has no `.data` property and its JSON body is never read. `const token = res?.data` is therefore undefined and `token.access_token` throws a TypeError. The catch block treats any non-`invalid_grant` message as recoverable and returns the old auth object, so synced Google credentials can never be refreshed and silently keep using an expired token.

findings.title: prisma is used without being imported
findings.body: The newly added refresh block calls `prisma.credential.update(...)`, but this file has no `prisma` import (imports are only jsforce, RRule, zod, helpers, types, getAppKeysFromSlug and parseRefreshTokenResponse). This is a TypeScript compile error and, if transpiled without checking, a runtime ReferenceError on every Salesforce client creation, breaking the Salesforce integration entirely.

findings.title: Salesforce connection is built with the stale pre-refresh access token
findings.body: After fetching and persisting a refreshed token, `new jsforce.Connection` is constructed with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` and `refreshToken: credentialKey.refresh_token` — the old values from before the refresh, not `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`. The service therefore continues calling Salesforce with the expired token it just tried to replace. The refresh is also performed unconditionally on every `getClient` call, even when the stored token is still valid.

findings.title: Credential ID is passed where refreshOAuthTokens expects userId
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(refreshFn, appSlug, userId)` sends its third argument as `calcomUserId` to the sync endpoint and only enables sync when it is truthy. This caller passes `credentialId` (the credential's primary key, threaded through `refreshAccessToken(credentialId, ...)`) instead of `credential.userId`. The parent platform will be asked for tokens for the wrong user (or a non-existent user whose id equals the credential id), returning wrong/no credentials.

findings.title: Webhook handler has no error handling or method check
findings.body: The handler accepts any HTTP method and calls `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` (line 31) and `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` (lines 57-59) with no try/catch. Malformed JSON, an invalid body, or undecryptable `keys` throws an unhandled exception resulting in an opaque 500 (and potentially a stack-bearing error response) instead of a 400, and non-POST requests are processed the same as POST. There are also no tests for this new credential-writing endpoint.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time string inequality
findings.body: The shared secret that authorizes overwriting any user's third-party credentials is checked with `!==` on line 25-27, which short-circuits on the first differing byte and is susceptible to timing attacks. A secret protecting credential write access should be compared in constant time (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual` after length checks).
